'''Joseph R. Dwyer''' (born 1963) is an American physicist known for his lightning research. He is a professor of physics at the [[University of New Hampshire]]. Dwyer received his Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1994 and worked on [[cosmic-ray]] physics and [[gamma-ray]] astronomy as a research scientist at [[Columbia University]] and the [[University of Maryland]] before joining the faculty at the [[Florida Institute of Technology]] in 2000. After moving to [[Melbourne, Florida]], Dwyer became interested in [[lightning]] physics and his research now focuses on high-energy radiation production from [[thunderstorms]] and [[lightning]]. In 2002, Dwyer and collaborators discovered that rocket-triggered lightning produced large quantities of [[x-rays]], allowing for first the time detailed studies of an atmospheric phenomenon known as [[runaway breakdown]]. In 2014, Dwyer left the Florida Institute of Technology and joined the University of New Hampshire.

==Research==
In 2002 Dwyer, along with colleagues from Florida Institute of Technology and the [[University of Florida]], launched rockets during thunderstorms at a facility now known as the UF/Florida Tech International Center for Lightning Research and Testing (ICLRT) at [[Camp Blanding, Florida]]. Using a heavily shielded instrument containing a [[scintillation detector]], built by Dwyer and his students, they found that lightning does indeed produce x-rays and that x-ray emission is common for lightning. This research was published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' (Dwyer et al. 2003).<ref name= "Energetic Radiation Produced During Rocket Triggered-Lightning">{{cite journal |url= field of High Energy Atmospheric Physics, including work on runaway electron or [[runaway breakdown]] physics,<ref name= "A fundamental limit on electric fields in air">{{cite news |url= May 2009|archive-date= 10 June 2009|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090610040953/http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2009/2008JD011386.shtml|url-status= dead}}</ref> and lightning initiation.<ref name= "A fundamental limit on electric fields in air"/> In 2003, he introduced the Relativistic Feedback Mechanism of [[relativistic-runaway-electron avalanche]]s,<ref name= "Source mechanisms of terrestrial gamma-ray flashes">{{cite news |url= http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2008/2007JD009248.shtml |title= Source mechanisms of terrestrial gamma-ray flashes |work= Journal of Geophysical Research |date= 20 May 2008 |accessdate= 20 May 2008 |archive-date= 1 November 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111101061036/http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2008/2007JD009248.shtml |url-status= dead }}</ref> a new discharge mechanism in air, which explains how thunderclouds may generate very large flashes of gamma-rays called [[terrestrial gamma-ray flashes]] (TGFs).<ref name= "Physics">{{cite news |url= http://physics.aps.org/articles/v4/1 |title= Chance of thunder—and gamma-ray flashes |work= Physics |date= 3 January 2011 |accessdate= 3 January 2011}}</ref>  This work also showed the importance of [[positrons]] (anti-electrons) for thundercloud electrodynamics.  Working with David Smith from UCSC he also helped establish that TGFs originate from deep within our atmosphere and not at high altitudes as had been previously assumed.  Indeed, Dwyer and his team observed a ground level TGF at Camp Blanding in 2004.<ref name= "A ground level gamma-ray burst observed in association with rocket-triggered lightning">{{cite news |url= http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2004/2003GL018771.shtml |title= A ground level gamma-ray burst observed in association with rocket-triggered lightning |work= Geophysical Research Letters |date= 13 March 2004 |accessdate= 13 March 2004 |archive-date= 10 May 2004 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20040510155748/http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2004/2003GL018771.shtml |url-status= dead }}</ref>  Finally, using BATSE data from the Compton Gamma-ray Observatory, Dwyer and collaborators discovered Terrestrial Electron Beams (TEBs) <ref name= "High-energy electron beams launched into space by thunderstorms">{{cite news |url= http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2008/2007GL032430.shtml |title= High-energy electron beams launched into space by thunderstorms |work= Geophysical Research Letters |date= 31 January 2008 |accessdate= 31 January 2008 |archive-date= 16 February 2008 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080216015510/http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2008/2007GL032430.shtml |url-status= dead }}</ref> in the inner magnetosphere, which are generated by the high energy emissions from thunderstorms.

==Achievements==
Dwyer has written and/or co-authored over 100 scientific research papers, more than 40 of them on lightning, terrestrial gamma-ray flashes, and x-rays from lightning.  He has provided content to the PBS/NOVA website on lightning.<ref name= "Lightning: Expert Q&A">{{cite news |url= https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/dwyer-lightning/  |title= Lightning: Expert Q&A |work= NOVA |date= 1 October 2005 |access-date= 1 October 2005}}</ref> He has spoken at many university colloquia, conferences, and workshops on his work. His work has also appeared on multiple documentaries, including Nova ScienceNow,<ref name= "NOVA|How Lightning works">{{cite news |url= https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/how-lightning-works/ |title= How Lightning Works |work= NOVA |date= 1 October 2005 |access-date= 1 October 2005}}</ref> Discovery Channel,<ref name= "Discovery News: Cosmic Rays">{{cite news |url= http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2009/06/09/lightning-cosmic-rays.html |title= Cosmic Rays Could Reveal Why Lightning Strikes |work= Discovery News |date= 9 June 2009 |accessdate= 9 June 2009}}</ref> the weather channel and BBC.<ref name= "BBC News - Antimatter caught">{{cite news |url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-12158718   |title= Antimatter caught streaming from thunderstorms on Earth |work= BBC News |date= 11 January 2011 |accessdate= 11 January 2011}}</ref> Dwyer is the director of the Geospace Physics Lab at [[Florida Institute of Technology]], advisor of graduate students, a member of the [[American Geophysical Union]], and helps Florida Institute of Technology jointly operate the International Center for Lightning Research and Testing with the [[University of Florida]] lightning research group.

Dwyer was named a Fellow of the American Geophysical Union in 2019.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=2019 Class of AGU Fellows Announced|url=https://eos.org/agu-news/2019-class-of-agu-fellows-announced|access-date=2020-06-19|journal=Eos|year=2019|language=en-US|doi=10.1029/2019eo131029|last1=Bell|first1=Robin|last2=Holmes|first2=Mary|volume=100|doi-access=free}}</ref>
